title: Right-sizing & Burst Simulation — HyperGrid Systems technical deep dive
summary: Deep technical session on autoscaling and capacity planning. Covered queueing models, burst policies, reserved GPU sizing, eviction/TTL for KV cache, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run two synthetic burst sims and a 48h pilot on a dedicated pool; Redwood to provide a capacity-simulator spreadsheet and suggested configs for KV eviction and batching targets.
topics: burst policies and burst budget sizing
KV cache eviction policies and prefix caching
quantization impacts on latency (int8, 4-bit) and quality
VPC/on-prem networking constraints and cross-AZ routing

transcript:
MEETING HEADER:
Date: 2025-07-21
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Solution Arch), Marta (Redwood CS Ops); Lena (HyperGrid Head of ML), Tom (Infra), Priya (CTO), Marcus (SRE)

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick run of the agenda — we want to validate burst behavior, sizing for reserved gpus, and go over kv cache eviction and batching. are there any other items?

[00:18] Lena: no, that's good. main ask is predictable p95 latency under 2s for our chat endpoint at 1k concurrent users, and we need the budget to be reasonable.

[00:33] Sofia: perfect. we'll walk through the simulator and then talk about the policy knobs — burst budget, queue depth, max outstanding requests, and eviction for the kv. i might drop into the runtime internals.

[00:48] Tom: one thing to flag — our infra is multi-AZ in us-west-2, but we have strict egress limits so cross-AZ fallbacks are not ideal. also prefer VPC peering rather than internet egress for private deployment.

[01:05] Jordan: noted. that will affect routing policy and fallback tiers — keep that in mind when we suggest cross-region fallbacks.

[01:22] Sofia: quick overview: Redwood's serving runtime supports continuous batching, prefix kv cache, and adaptive kernel selection. for autoscale we expose: reserved pool size, burst_capacity (seconds of sustained QPS above baseline), and max_queue_depth. behind the scenes we use a token-bucket style admission + backpressure.

[01:40] Marcus: when you say token-bucket, is that per-model or per-pool?

[01:47] Sofia: per-pool. each pool has a token rate matching steady-state throughput. burst tokens accumulate up to burst_capacity which is in seconds of throughput. when tokens deplete, new requests can be queued up to max_queue_depth, after which we will start rejecting or redirecting to fallback models depending on policy.

[02:05] Priya: what's a realistic burst_capacity — how many seconds should we buy?

[02:11] Ethan: common patterns we see: customer-facing chat apps with spiky traffic typically configure 30–120s of burst capacity. longer is safer but obviously more costly because you need idle reserved GPUs or pre-warmed instances for that headroom.

[02:28] Tom: so if we set 60s burst, and our steady throughput is 500 rps, that means we need capacity to handle 500 * 60 = 30k requests in the burst window? that seems huge.

[02:42] Sofia: small clarification — burst_capacity is measured in 'seconds at baseline throughput' which lets the pool handle additional short-term load without immediately provisioning new hardware. it isn't a literal request buffer of 30k; it's more like we allow 60s of extra serving headroom before autoscaler triggers allocation. we still have queue limits.

[03:03] Lena: can you walk through the queuing model? we care about p95 tail.

[03:10] Sofia: yes. simplified model: we treat the pool as M/M/c for queuing math intuition (Poisson arrivals, exponential service). with batching and concurrency, effective service rate varies by sequence length and batching efficiency. continuous batching increases throughput but also adds a small batching latency. we run the numbers with a simulator that models real request size distribution.

[03:32] Jordan: we also include KV cache hit/miss behavior in the sim; a hit short-circuits many decoder steps, reducing service time materially. so TTL and eviction policy for the kv cache changes the effective service rate.

[03:45] Tom: what eviction policy do you recommend? we have limited RAM on the inference nodes.

[03:52] Sofia: for chat workloads with repeating prefixes, LRU with a small bias to pin recent conversation prefixes works well. LFU can be better if you have hot stable prefixes across many users. we usually recommend LRU with a 6–24 hour TTL for conversational caches, and a hot-set reserve for very frequent prompts.

[04:12] Lena: and the sizes? how much KV capacity per GPU?

[04:18] Sofia: ballpark: on A100 like shapes, typical kv state (per active convo) ~ 2–6KB for medium-length contexts; we size 8–16GB of shared KV per GPU to support 10s of thousands of warm prefixes. on smaller GPUs numbers change — but that's the rough heuristic.

[04:37] Marcus: that seems expensive. can we evict aggressively and rely on cold starts?

[04:42] Sofia: yes, but cold misses increase decoding steps and p95 increases. tradeoff: aggressive eviction reduces memory but increases cost-per-query due to longer decode time and increased compute. quantization also affects this — a smaller model or int8 path has fewer params in memory which helps.

[05:02] Priya: let's talk quantization — we plan to run q4_k_m for the smaller models and int8 for the larger. what's the latency delta?

[05:11] Sofia: quantization reduces memory footprint and can slightly improve throughput, but kernel selection matters. int8 usually reduces per-token latency by 10–30% depending on the op and hardware support; non-native 4-bit paths sometimes add some kernel overhead but reduce memory massively. our runtime chooses optimized kernels; we'll include per-model perf numbers in the simulator CSV.

[05:37] Tom: about continuous batching — we saw in our internal tests that batching sometimes adds 50–120ms. we need to keep p95 < 2s. is that feasible with batching?

[05:47] Jordan: yes, batching tradeoffs depend on arrival rates. continuous batching uses a short batching window (e.g., 10–30ms) and can combine idle tokens to increase throughput with minimal added latency. when you have high concurrency, batching overhead amortizes across requests. for low QPS steady-state, batching adds relative overhead.

[06:06] Lena: can you share a concrete example where p95 stays under 2s for 1k concurrent users?

[06:13] Sofia: we ran a synthetic on similar profile: steady-state 600 rps, spikes to 2.5k for ~45s. with a reserved pool of 8 A100 equiv GPUs, burst_capacity 60s, max_queue_depth 500, and KV hit-rate ~ 65%, p95 was ~1.7s. with kv hit-rate drop to 20%, p95 moved to ~2.4s. so cache hit-rate is huge for tail.

[06:42] Tom: how does the autoscaler react? do we spin new GPUs mid-burst?

[06:48] Sofia: autoscaler has two modes: proactive (start spinning based on queue growth heuristics) and reactive (allocate when tokens/burst budget are exhausted). spin-up time for GPUs depends on environment — in Dedicated we can keep warm spare nodes (hot standbys) to reduce spin up to ~30–90s; in Private/on-prem it's usually slower. hence the importance of burst_capacity.

[07:10] Marcus: about warm standbys — what's the billing model? do we pay for reserved capacity even when idle?

[07:16] Ethan: Reserved pools are monthly commitments; you pay for the reserved capacity. We provide flexible burst and burst pool options — burst instances can be pre-warmed at lower cost if you commit. we'll map cost in the spreadsheet.

[07:29] Priya: VPC/on-prem — how much of this changes if we host in our VPC or on-prem?

[07:36] Jordan: the runtime and autoscaler work the same but operational constraints differ. on-prem spin-up times are longer, image provisioning can add minutes, and KMS/HSM integrations may add handshake latency. also cross-AZ fallbacks are more rigid with VPC peering rules — you need routes allowed. we also recommend local caching nodes for KV to reduce cross-host calls.

[07:58] Tom: do you support local-only KV affinity? we want cached prefixes to be local to a GPU rack if possible.

[08:04] Sofia: yes, we have a locality-aware KV placement option — prefer local node caches, then rack, then global. that reduces cross-host traffic but increases risk of cold misses if traffic shifts. it's a config knob in Private deployments.

[08:20] Lena: more on queueing math — you mentioned M/M/c earlier. are we using that to size queues or a more sophisticated sim?

[08:27] Sofia: the sim uses empirical distributions and discrete-event sim to account for batching, kv hits, and kernel variance. M/M/c is an intuition floor for quick calcs. we'll share the simulator CSV with request size histogram, kv hit/miss latencies, and service time distributions.

[08:45] Marcus: what about request prioritization? we have admin traffic that must never be queued more than 200ms.

[08:52] Sofia: we support per-route priorities and token reservations. you can reserve a portion of tokens for high-priority routes so they bypass burst queueing and get immediate scheduling up to a threshold. that plays into queue depth and burst math.

[09:06] Tom: ejection policies — when nodes are overloaded, do you evict user prefixes or whole conversations?

[09:12] Sofia: eviction is per-prefix. we can evict LRU prefixes first or evict by conversation age. we also support a hot-set reserve where top-k prefixes are pinned. policies are pluggable.

[09:24] Priya: okay let's go through a hypothetical configuration that you would suggest for us given our constraints: p95 < 2s, multi-AZ with limited cross-AZ, budget conscious, baseline 500 rps, spikes to 2500 rps for ~1 min, mostly chat with some long contexts.

[09:44] Sofia: recommended baseline config: reserved pool = 10 A100-eq (this assumes 10k steady concurrency — we'll fine tune), burst_capacity = 90s, max_queue_depth = 600, KV policy = LRU with 12h TTL + hot-set reserve 5% of memory, batching window = 20ms, priority reservation 10% tokens for admin traffic. quantize large model to int8, run small model q4_k_m for low-cost fallback.

[10:11] Lena: that feels like a lot of reserved GPUs relative to budget. can you show cost tradeoffs?

[10:18] Ethan: yes that's exactly what the spreadsheet is for — we provide cost per-hour with different reserved counts and burst budgets. often a hybrid — smaller reserved pool + slightly longer burst capacity + pre-warmed carriers can be cost efficient versus heavy reserved. we'll model both.

[10:37] Jordan: also consider routing policy: route to cheaper q4 model for non-critical routes or when p95 threatens to breach. degrade gracefully.

[10:47] Tom: curious about queuing backpressure — if queue depth hits 600, do you reject? what's the rejection behavior? 4xx? 503? do you provide retry hints?

[10:55] Sofia: we return 429 when client should retry; we can also stream partial responses for long-polling scenarios. for strict SLAs you can set automatic fallback to a cheaper model rather than rejecting. we surface retry-after headers.

[11:08] Priya: let's talk about the pilot: you'd want to run a 48-hour pilot — what metrics will you collect?

[11:15] Ethan: we'll collect p50/p95/p99 latency, token-level cost, KV hit-rate, queue depth over time, autoscale events (spin-up/spin-down times), and any rejections. we also instrument GPU utilization and batching efficiency.

[11:26] Lena: and what success criteria should we use?

[11:29] Sofia: success = p95 < 2s for 95% of the traffic during simulated spikes, KV hit-rate > 50% for chat routes, and no more than X% of requests experiencing retry (we'll suggest a threshold). also cost per 1k requests within your target.

[11:45] Tom: any gotchas for Private on-prem? e.g., filesystem mounts, NFS, local NVMe?

[11:52] Jordan: yes: kernel modules, driver versions, and local NVMe caching cause most production surprises. pre-provisioning images and testing warm-up is critical. we recommend a staging run identical to prod for a week.

[12:06] Marcus: for the capacity simulator — can we run it with our real traces?

[12:10] Sofia: absolutely. Tom, if you upload the traces we'll plug them into the sim and return a stitch of predicted p95 curve and recommended pool size options.

[12:19] Tom: will do. one other: we have strict SOC2 requirements — do you capture audit logs for autoscale events and config changes?

[12:27] Marta: yes, we keep audit logs for scaling events, config changes, and admin actions. in Private you can forward to your SIEM or use our retention add-on.

[12:38] Priya: any final notes on kernel selection? sometimes certain ops are slower on older GPUs.

[12:43] Sofia: the runtime picks kernels based on architecture. we profile models and recommend hardware. for us-west-2 A100s are usually the sweet spot for quantized ints. for lower cost T4/RTX style nodes, more quantization and smaller batch targets help.

[12:59] Ethan: quick recap and actions — we'll send the simulator, a recommended KV config, and charge model spreadsheet. HyperGrid will provide traces and confirm pilot window.

[13:10] Lena: thanks, appreciate the depth. we'll review and get the traces uploaded.

[13:18] Ethan: great. any final questions?

[13:22] Tom: none from infra.

[13:24] Marcus: all good.

[13:26] Priya: thank you.

[13:30] Ethan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in an email with links.

END TRANSCRIPT

NOTES ON TRANSCRIPTION QUALITY: occasional mis-heard acronyms (e.g., q4_k_m transcribed as q4-km), some speaker labels approximated, punctuation irregularities.
